story: The garage door opener broke last week, and I watched my seventy-year-old father struggling to lift it manually, his face reddening with effort, because he hadn't gotten around to calling a repairman. He hadn't gotten around to it because he was covering my car insurance. The math was simple and damning. I jumped up to help, and we lifted together in silence. His breathing was labored. When had he gotten this old? While he was raising me, probably, then working to prepare for a retirement that now included supporting his grown son again. I called the repairman myself that afternoon, paced the driveway while on hold, did the mental calculation of whether my checking account could cover it. It could, barely, if I skipped looking for apartments this month.

topic: An adult child moves back in with their parents
story: She found her mother's journal—not snooping, just misplaced on the bathroom counter. The page was open, and one line caught her eye before she could look away: "I worry we failed her somehow." The words punched the air from her lungs. She set the journal down carefully, exactly as she'd found it, her fingers trembling. That evening, she offered to cook dinner, something she hadn't done since moving back. She burned the chicken, overcooked the vegetables, but her parents ate every bite and complimented the meal. Her father even asked for seconds. The knot in her throat made it hard to swallow her own food. She wanted to tell them it wasn't their fault, that her failures were her own, but the words wouldn't form. Instead, she cleared the table and washed dishes until the water ran cold.

topic: An adult child moves back in with their parents
story: I started sleeping in my car some nights, parked a few blocks away, telling myself I needed the space but knowing it was really about giving them space. About not being underfoot every single moment. When I sneak back in at dawn, I can see the light already on in the kitchen—Mom's up, probably has been for hours, probably noticed my car was gone and spent the night worrying. I slip in quietly, but she calls out anyway, offers breakfast. I decline, say I ate already, another lie to add to the collection. She nods, and something in her expression—resignation, maybe, or understanding—makes me want to sink through the floor. I head upstairs and finally notice the new photos she's hung in the hallway: me at various ages, accomplishments she's still proud of. I can't remember the last time I gave her a reason to add to that collection.
